```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(univariateML)
```

## Fit and calculate standard errors

`vcov()` returns covariance in the coefficients' natural units. The default
`"sandwich"` uses individual observation scores and observed information;
`"observed"` returns inverse observed information and assumes a correctly
specified model. Both require appropriate regularity and large-sample
estimator behavior. Sandwich inference under misspecification additionally
requires independent observations, a well-defined pseudo-true parameter,
finite score variance and nonsingular sensitivity. It is not protection
against arbitrary outliers, dependence or infinite score variance.

```{r covariance}
set.seed(10210)
x <- rnorm(200, mean = 2, sd = 1)
fit <- mlnorm(x)
V <- vcov(fit)                       # sandwich (default)
V_model <- vcov(fit, type = "observed")
cbind(estimate = as.numeric(fit),
      sandwich_se = sqrt(diag(V)),
      observed_se = sqrt(diag(V_model)))
attr(V, "condition")
attr(V, "validity_conditions")
```

The diagonal entries are variances; their square roots are standard errors.
Matrix row and column names identify the coefficients. No extra division by
sample size is needed. These standard errors do not change `confint()`, which
uses a parametric bootstrap. Neither method guarantees finite-sample coverage.

## Held coefficients and nuisance parameters

```{r held}
known_mean <- mlnorm(x, mean = 2)
V_known <- vcov(known_mean)
rownames(V_known)                     # only sd is free
attr(V_known, "held")                # mean is treated as known
sqrt(diag(V_known))

all_known <- mlnorm(x, mean = 2, sd = 1)
dim(vcov(all_known))                 # 0 by 0: no free coefficients
```

Holding a coefficient conditions on its supplied value. Holding an estimated
nuisance coefficient at its fitted value would discard its uncertainty. If a
nuisance coefficient was estimated, keep it free and extract the desired
block from the full covariance. Fully held fits with observations return an
empty matrix; data-free frozen distributions cannot supply covariance.
Older saved fits without retained observations must be refitted. Keep the
original fit's coefficients, order and inference attributes intact.

## Errors and conditioning

Availability depends on the family, parameter regime and free subset. For
example, estimating uniform endpoints does not permit this regular covariance:

```{r unavailable}
tryCatch(vcov(mlunif(c(0.2, 0.5, 0.9))),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

An unavailable family, subset or regime means this procedure is unsupported;
it does not imply that every possible confidence procedure is invalid.
Boundary or limit fits outside supported conditional submodels are rejected,
as are fits on a fitting restriction.
Invalid observations, nonfinite numerical derivatives, singular, indefinite
or excessively ill-conditioned information also cause errors with a reason.
A fit can therefore succeed while `vcov()` fails. Do not replace that error
with an optimizer's inverse Hessian or a pseudoinverse.

A successful solve warns when the observed-information eigenvalue condition
number exceeds $10^6$. This diagnostic uses natural coefficient units, so it
changes with measurement scale. It indicates numerical sensitivity, rather
than testing statistical validity. Rescaling data and refitting in suitable
units may help numerical conditioning; transform the resulting covariance
back to the desired coordinates. The absence of a warning is no validity check.

## When Wald uncertainty is unreliable

At the skew-normal (`sn`) member `alpha = 0`, joint information is singular
when location is free. Bhattacharjee (`bhatt`) fits near `a = 0` approach a
normal member with weakly identified width. Even accepted fits near these
members can have unstable standard errors. Holding a parameter known defines
a different submodel and needs its own validity conditions.

Small samples can weakly identify several shape parameters: observed and
sandwich standard errors can differ substantially even under the fitted
model. Heavy tails can slow convergence or violate the score-moment assumptions.
An infinite observation variance alone does not imply infinite score variance;
the relevant moments depend on the model and free coefficients.

The inference catalogue at `/inference/` on the companion documentation site
lists procedure availability by regime and free subset. Consult that page and
the family's dossier for supported subsets and conditions. Monte Carlo
comparisons of standard errors with empirical sampling variability are
numerical evidence at the tested points, not proofs of regularity, Wald
coverage or robustness under misspecification.
